mission.mission_purpose: Today's Mission exists to extend yesterday's exploratory craft into bivariate association. So you can select and interpret Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall measures without confusing correlation with causation or with identical information.
mission.tutor_intent: Today I will force the candidate to say what each correlation measure is sensitive to, and to refuse a causal claim from a coefficient alone. So association stays exploratory inference, not storytelling.
mission.educational_intent: Produce a cognitive move from 'correlation is one number' to 'I can choose among Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall for the data situation and state what the coefficient does and does not justify.'
mission.learning_objective: Interpret Pearson's, Spearman's, and Kendall's correlation measures for bivariate data and state the inferential limits of each choice.
mission.concept_focus: Measure choice → what association means → what it does not mean (causation / linearity assumptions).
mission.prior_bridge: Yesterday you defended summaries and visualisations for a stated aim under 1.2.1. Today those explored variables become a bivariate pair: you interpret association measures with the same aim discipline.
mission.why_now: 1.2.2 is the next LO after tool judgement; examiners require correct measure choice and honest interpretation; PCA (1.2.3) is deferred so association is learned cleanly before dimensionality reduction.
mission.expected_benefit: One justified measure choice and one honest limit statement. Study Progress for today's Session, not Topic Complete for all of 1.2 including PCA.
mission.explainability: Assigned as Campaign Alpha Day 3 because Day 2 established exploratory description; the skill gap now is disciplined association under LO 1.2.2.
success_criteria: Closed-book, distinguish Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall in one sentence each (what each primarily captures).
For a stated data situation, choose one measure and justify why it fits.
State one claim the coefficient does not support (e.g. causation or perfect predictive control).
task_descriptions: Sketch Pearson / Spearman / Kendall as three boxes with one sensitivity note each before opening the CMP.
Complete Guided Reading through CMP treatment of the three correlation measures (1.2.2 centre).
Closed-book: distinguish, choose, and refuse an overclaim.

session.session_educational_purpose: This Session exists to execute today's Mission: build and stress-test closed-book interpretation of Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall. Not to begin PCA or full inferential modelling.
session.session_tutor_purpose: In this hour I will set focus questions on measure differences and limits, exit for CMP work on 1.2.2, then retrieve distinguish–choose–refuse-overclaim. So association is tested as judgement.

knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: three measures
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly distinguishes Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation and names one rank-versus-Pearson difference?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: The three measures answer related but different association questions; treating them as synonyms fails examiner discrimination.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Pearson linear raw; Spearman monotonic ranks; Kendall concordance; ranks more robust for monotone nonlinear or some outlier cases.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Saying only that they all measure correlation without discrimination.

choices.label: Pearson measures linear association of raw values. Spearman measures monotonic association via ranks. Kendall measures pairwise concordance of orderings. Rank measures are more robust to some nonlinear monotone relationships and some outlier patterns than Pearson.
Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall all measure the same linear association of raw values, so choosing among them is only a naming preference.
Pearson is rank-based and robust to outliers, while Spearman and Kendall measure only linear association of raw values.
Kendall measures causation, Spearman measures prediction accuracy, and Pearson measures only sample size.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: choose and refuse overclaim
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Two skewed positive variables show outliers and a roughly increasing but nonlinear scatter. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Choose measure preference and refuse an overclaim.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Measure choice follows shape and robustness; interpretation discipline refuses causal theatre from exploratory association.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Prefer Spearman or Kendall for monotone nonlinear association with outliers; refuse causation from the coefficient.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Choosing Pearson by habit, or claiming causation from r.

choices.label: Prefer Spearman or Kendall because the relationship looks monotone but nonlinear with outliers that can distort Pearson. A large coefficient still does not prove that changing X causes Y to change.
Prefer Pearson by habit for every numeric pair, and treat a large r as proof that changing X causes Y.
Any correlation measure is interchangeable here, and a large coefficient justifies controlling Y by changing X.
Prefer Spearman only when the scatter is perfectly linear with no outliers, and refuse rank measures when skew is present.

worked_example.title: Choose Spearman for monotone nonlinear mileage association
worked_example.problem_statement: For annual mileage versus claim severity, severity is skewed with outliers and the scatter looks roughly increasing but nonlinear. Software reports Pearson r = 0.25 and Spearman ρ = 0.52. Which correlation measure should you prefer for describing the association, and what must you still refuse?

given.value: roughly increasing, nonlinear; skewed severity with outliers

worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Match measure to linear vs monotone-nonlinear association, then separate association from causation.

steps.label: Match measure to association type
steps.attempt_cue: Say what Pearson vs Spearman each target.
steps.explanation: Pearson measures linear association. Spearman uses ranks and suits monotone but nonlinear patterns, with better resistance to outliers in many skewed cases.
steps.calculation: Pattern = monotone nonlinear + outliers → prefer Spearman (or Kendall)

steps.label: Read the two reported coefficients
steps.attempt_cue: Compare |r| and |ρ| in light of the scatter.
steps.explanation: The weaker Pearson value is expected when the relationship is not linear. The stronger Spearman value better reflects the monotone increase under skew and outliers.
steps.calculation: |ρ| = 0.52 > |r| = 0.25; rank measure captures monotone association better here
steps.result: Report Spearman ρ = 0.52 as the preferred description

steps.label: Refuse causation from correlation
steps.attempt_cue: State what a large coefficient still does not prove.
steps.explanation: A large correlation coefficient does not prove that changing mileage causes severity to change.
steps.result: Refuse causal claim from correlation alone

worked_example.final_answer: Prefer Spearman ρ = 0.52 (monotone, skewed, outlier-prone) over Pearson r = 0.25. A large coefficient still does not prove causation.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Defaulting to Pearson because it is the familiar default, or treating Spearman ρ = 0.52 as proof that higher mileage causes higher claim severity.
